name: PlanetScale
tagline: Operate a small MySQL-compatible database with migrations and backups on one server

pricing.notes: Typical entry paid database package; usage terms apply.

tiers.name: Base - single-node Postgres
tiers.limits: Starts at $5/month; single-node Postgres; 10 GB included egress.
tiers.notes: Resource size and storage determine the final amount.

tiers.name: Base - high-availability Postgres
tiers.limits: Starts at $15/month for a 3-node HA configuration; 100 GB included egress.
tiers.notes: Published starting example uses three PS-5 ARM nodes.

tiers.name: Metal
tiers.limits: Starts at $50/month for dedicated-metal database compute.
tiers.notes: Resource size, replicas and storage determine the final amount.

tiers.name: Vitess
tiers.limits: Resource-based MySQL/Vitess pricing; exact public starting total is not exposed as one fixed plan price.

tiers.name: Enterprise
tiers.limits: Custom resources, security, support and contract terms.

pricing.billingTerms: monthly pay as you go for Base and Metal; Enterprise custom; no public annual self-serve plan
pricing.hiddenCosts: Egress above the included amount is $0.06/GB; extra production branches duplicate the selected cluster cost. Development branches include 2x the month's hours and then cost about $0.014/hour; HA storage can effectively cost $1.50/GB because it is replicated across 3 nodes. SSO and support can be add-ons.

verdictSummary: A consolation build is possible, but the paid product's decisive value sits outside a solo rebuild. For PlanetScale, operate a small MySQL-compatible database with migrations and backups on one server. The hard boundary is vitess operations, branching, nonblocking schema workflow, scale, and support, plus infrastructure scale, operations, and reliability.
coreLoopDIY: Operate a small MySQL-compatible database on one user-owned server, run schema migrations, retain logs, and perform regular backups.
whatYouLose: Vitess operations, branching, nonblocking schema workflow, scale, and support
ongoingBurden: patching, certificates, isolation, secrets, builds, deploys, logs, metrics, backups, capacity, incidents, and security response
whyPeopleStillPay: People still pay for PlanetScale because hosting products sell an operations team and failure-domain diversity, not merely a deploy button. The recurring cost buys patching, certificates, isolation, secrets, builds, deploys, logs, metrics, backups, capacity, incidents, and security response, not just the visible interface.

priorArt.name: Coolify
priorArt.desc: Active open-source self-hosting platform for applications, databases, and services.

alternatives.name: Coolify
alternatives.desc: A MySQL container with TLS, monitoring, scheduled backups, and restore controls on one server; branching is gone with PlanetScale.

alternatives.name: Dokploy
alternatives.desc: Run MySQL on your own host with managed deployment and backups; schema branching is the thing you give up.

rejectedAlternatives.name: Dokku
rejectedAlternatives.desc: The MySQL plugin deploys a database, but migrations and dependable backups are still your scripts.

notes: Editorial comparison targets the Scaler Pro plan and a single-server personal platform DIY substitute. Recheck price before merge.
prompt:
Build a closest honest personal substitute for PlanetScale in an empty repository.
Use Docker Compose, Caddy, PostgreSQL, Redis, and a small Go control plane; do not offer alternative stacks.
The core loop is: operate a small MySQL-compatible database on one user-owned server, run schema migrations, retain logs, and perform regular backups.
Make the first run work locally with one documented command.
Store all user data locally by default and make export straightforward.
Put secrets in .env, ship .env.example, and never commit credentials.
Accept a Git repository or container image and one explicit Dockerfile-based build path.
Implement applications, environments, secrets, domains, health checks, and rolling container replacement.
Use Caddy for automatic TLS and route only to healthy local containers.
Capture bounded build and runtime logs and expose restart, rollback, and redeploy actions.
Back up PostgreSQL metadata and document backups for each deployed application's data volumes.
Add host metrics, disk alerts, update instructions, disaster recovery, and a prominent single-server warning.
Include clear empty, loading, success, and recoverable error states.
Add input validation, safe filenames, and graceful handling of unavailable APIs.
Write focused tests for the core transformation and one end-to-end happy path.
Create a README with setup, architecture, permissions, data location, and backup steps.
Do not add accounts, billing, telemetry, analytics, or a hosted control plane.
Do not claim to reproduce proprietary data, network liquidity, regulated access, or frontier infrastructure.
Deliberately leave out multi-region or serverless infrastructure.
Deliberately leave out managed data stores and global edge delivery.
Deliberately leave out DDoS response, compliance, and guaranteed uptime.
Finish by running the tests and listing the exact commands used.
